transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, thanks. I guess what finally made me come in is… over the past year or so, I’ve noticed I’m getting pulled off what I’m doing by the tiniest things. Like, I’ll be in my office trying to focus on something important, and my phone will buzz once, or someone will walk past the doorway, or even just some random thought pops in—like something about my in-laws, out of nowhere—and suddenly I’m off track before I even realize it.

It’s not like some huge dramatic thing, but it’s happening enough that I’m noticing it, and it’s frustrating because I’ll be trying to stay with one task and then, boom, I’m somewhere else mentally. I think that’s really what brought me here.
Thinking back, would you say you've always had some degree of this distractibility since childhood, or is this a new change from how you used to be able to focus?

Yeah, no, looking back I don’t think it’s totally new. I mean, it feels more noticeable now because I’ve got more responsibility and more things competing for my attention, but if I’m being honest, this kind of thing was around when I was a kid too.

Teachers were always moving my seat around in class. Like, I’d get put near the front, then away from certain kids, then by myself sometimes, because I talked too much or I’d get up without asking. And I remember blurting out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question, which I didn’t really think was a big deal at the time—I just felt like I knew what they were getting at and wanted to say it. But adults definitely seemed to notice it. So yeah, I’d say there’s been some version of it going way back.
Do you still notice things like feeling restless, needing to move around, or blurting things out impulsively in your day-to-day life now, as an adult?

Yeah, I do. Not constantly, but it comes up in situations where I’m expected to just sit there and be still. Like family dinners are a big one, or church volunteer meetings — places where you’re supposed to be calm and polite and just listen.

Inside, it feels like there’s this motor running, like I need to move or do something. I’ll be sitting there trying to pay attention, but my leg wants to bounce, or I’m shifting in the chair, or I’m messing with a napkin or a pen or whatever’s in front of me. It’s not even always because I want to leave or because I’m upset. It’s more like my body just doesn’t settle down the way other people’s seem to.

And I try to hide it, especially in church-related stuff or around family, because I don’t want to come across rude. But yeah, when I’m supposed to sit still, that restless feeling is definitely still there.
Would you say these difficulties with focus and restlessness have actually caused real problems for you—like at work, in your relationships, or with everyday responsibilities?

Yeah… I mean, I’m still functioning. That’s the weird part, I guess. From the outside, I’m keeping up overall — work is getting done, bills are paid, I show up for things. It’s not like everything has fallen apart.

But it is starting to cost me in ways that bother me. At work, especially in meetings or when I’m mentoring someone, I can tell people get frustrated if I jump ahead too fast or the conversation doesn’t go the way it should. Sometimes I lose the thread or push things in a direction too quickly, and I can feel people’s patience kind of thinning, even if they’re polite about it.

And at home, it’s more about trust, I think. Like with family plans, if I’m not fully locked in or I get sidetracked, it can come across like I don’t care or I’m not taking it seriously. I don’t mean it that way, but I know intent only goes so far. My family needs to feel like they can count on me to stay with the plan or follow the conversation, and lately I feel like I’m giving them reasons to doubt that.

So… real problems, yes, but mild ones maybe? I’m not crashing and burning, but it’s starting to create tension, and I don’t like where that could go if I just ignore it.
Can you think back to before you were about 12 years old—were these same kinds of restlessness and distractibility clearly present and causing noticeable problems for you at that age?

Yeah, before 12, definitely. I mean, I don’t have every grade perfectly mapped out in my head, but that pattern was there pretty clearly.

Teachers were moving my seat around a lot because I talked too much, or I’d get up when I wasn’t supposed to, or I’d blurt out answers before they even finished asking the question. I remember that happening enough that it wasn’t like a one-time “kid being a kid” thing. It was more like, “Okay, where do we put him so he’ll stop interrupting or moving around?”

At the time I didn’t really understand it as a problem. I just felt like I had something to say, or I knew the answer, or I needed to move. But looking back, yeah, adults were clearly reacting to it, and it caused enough disruption that they were changing where I sat and trying to manage me in class. So yes, this was definitely present before I was 12.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a longstanding pattern, present since early childhood (before age 12), of both inattentive symptoms (distractibility by minor external/internal stimuli, difficulty sustaining focus, losing track of conversations/tasks) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inner restlessness, fidgeting, difficulty remaining seated, blurting out answers, interrupting). Both symptom domains have persisted into adulthood, are present across multiple settings (work, home, social/religious gatherings), and are causing functional impairment in occupational performance and relational trust, though not severe. The combination of significant inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms with childhood onset and cross-situational impairment supports Combined Presentation ADHD (F90.2) over predominantly inattentive (F90.0) or predominantly hyperactive-impulsive (F90.1) subtypes.
